title: Same hours, different calendar
hook: Three hours in one block or across three days: what changes a month later?

knows: reading short labels and comparing simple counts
doesNotKnow: Separate the research-supported spacing effect from invented memory curves.

misconception: Equal study hours imply equal long-term recall regardless of calendar.
objective: Separate the research-supported spacing effect from invented memory curves.

claims.text: Scenario, hook and prediction: Three hours in one block or across three days: what changes a month later? For equal study time, which plan generally supports longer-term verbal recall? Correct option: Distributed sessions. All fixture labels, example words, dates, task durations and file fields are stipulated exercise data.
claims.source: Explicit exercise fixture in src/lib/lifehacks/studyCatalog.ts and pure rules in studyModels.ts. All times, sizes, deadlines and outcomes describe this exercise only; no empirical productivity or learning effect is inferred. FC LH-1 (session 2, received by message): verified; see company/reviews/lifehacks-200/fact-check-LH1-2026-10-14.md.

claims.text: Research on verbal recall supports distributed practice. The curves illustrate that idea; they do not predict your memory.
claims.source: Cepeda et al. (2006), Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks, Psychological Bulletin132(3),354–380, DOI10.1037/0033-2909.132.3.354, author abstract via https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16719566/ retrieved2026-10-13; 839 assessments in317 experiments. Rawson & Kintsch(2005), Rereading Effects Depend on Time of Test, JEP97(1),70–80, DOI10.1037/0022-0663.97.1.70, author abstract search record https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ688037 retrieved2026-10-13 (direct page timed out). Retrieval line supported separately by Roediger & Karpicke(2006), Roediger & Karpicke (2006), Test-Enhanced Learning, Psychological Science 17(3),249–255, DOI10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x; publisher abstract retrieved 2026-10-13: https://www.psychologicalscience.org/journals/psychological-science/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x/ . Prose-passage experiments found delayed retention advantages for retrieval over restudy. This short exercise does not establish that effect for the learner. FC LH-1 (session 2, received by message): verified; see company/reviews/lifehacks-200/fact-check-LH1-2026-10-14.md.

claims.text: Every displayed result is computed from the visible exercise state: spacing. Illustrative curves; not personal memory predictions. The reveal reports this same state and never translates its score into a personal productivity or memory benefit.
claims.source: src/lib/lifehacks/studyModels.ts and src/components/lifehacks/StudyLesson.tsx, spaced-beats-cram fixture in src/lib/lifehacks/studyCatalog.ts. Stage rules: cram=exp(-day/7), distributed=exp(-day/18); illustrative parameters, not fitted data. Marker visits gate the reveal; three sessions on days-2,-1,0 are calendar markers, not fitted review boosts. Future decay curves, scrub marker and retention-point markers are not rendered before prediction; only neutral stipulated calendars and chart axes are shown while locked. FC LH-1 (session 2, received by message): verified; see company/reviews/lifehacks-200/fact-check-LH1-2026-10-14.md.

claims.text: Massed rereading can perform better on an immediate test while distributed rereading can perform better on a delayed test; this does not establish the model curves or next-morning performance.
claims.source: Rawson & Kintsch(2005) author abstract via ERIC EJ688037. Retrieval is supported separately by Roediger & Karpicke(2006), publisher abstract. The lesson does not use Cepeda2006 as evidence for immediate-test reversal. FC LH-1 (session 2, received by message): verified; see company/reviews/lifehacks-200/fact-check-LH1-2026-10-14.md.

claims.text: Research on verbal recall generally favours spreading the same study time across sessions; total hours alone do not decide later recall.
claims.source: Cepeda et al. (2006), Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks, Psychological Bulletin 132(3), 354–380, DOI 10.1037/0033-2909.132.3.354, author abstract via https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16719566/ retrieved 2026-10-13; 839 assessments in 317 experiments. Rawson & Kintsch (2005), Rereading Effects Depend on Time of Test, JEP 97(1), 70–80, DOI 10.1037/0022-0663.97.1.70, author abstract search record https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ688037 retrieved 2026-10-13 (direct page timed out). Retrieval line supported separately by Roediger & Karpicke (2006), Test-Enhanced Learning, Psychological Science 17(3), 249–255, DOI 10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x; publisher abstract retrieved 2026-10-13: https://www.psychologicalscience.org/journals/psychological-science/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x/ . Prose-passage experiments found delayed retention advantages for retrieval over restudy. This short exercise does not establish that effect for the learner. Scenario values in the recall question are stipulated. Recall patch by learning-designer (session 2, 2026-10-14), applied by session 1. FC LH-3B (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): left unverified because the source could not be opened. The egress policy blocks pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov and the evullab.org author PDF (proxy 403). Search-result snippets agree with the cited abstract (839 assessments, 317 experiments, 184 articles; spacing benefits verbal recall; ISI and retention interval act jointly). The keyed option is the only one consistent with the source as cited, and the why is hedged ("generally"). Re-check from a connected host. See company/reviews/lifehacks-200/fact-check-LH3-2026-10-14.md (Batch B).

recall.question: You have four hours to learn vocabulary for a test in two weeks. Which plan fits the research this lesson summarises?
options: Four one-hour sessions on different days
One four-hour session the night before
Any split works; only total hours count
recall.why: Research on verbal recall generally favours spreading the same study time across sessions; total hours alone do not decide later recall.
